verses.1: Al-Mizan explains that the question is rhetorical and denies that people who merely say, “We have faith,” can be left without a test that reveals whether they are truthful. An yaqūlū conveys causation: they do not escape testing simply because of this assertion. Here fitna means examination (imtiḥān), not primarily affliction or persecution; the interpretation that it promises believers freedom from all tribulation is unlikely in light of the surrounding verses.

verses.3:
Al-Mizan notes that both emphatic lāms express an oath. The clause, “Certainly We tested those who were before them,” may qualify either “the people” or “they will not be tested”; the former is more fitting, since the rebuke concerns their expectation of exemption despite God’s established practice of testing people. This divine habit has applied to earlier peoples and will apply to them without change.

God’s “knowledge” of the truthful and the liars means that tests bring the practical effects of truthfulness and falsehood into view, according to whether faith is truly rooted in the heart. Happiness and divine reward follow real faith, manifested in patience under hardship, persistence in obedience, and steadfast avoidance of sin, rather than a mere profession of faith. Perhaps this is God’s knowledge as an act (al-ʿilm al-fiʿlī), identical with objective fact (nafs al-amr al-khārijī), whereas His essential knowledge (al-ʿilm al-dhātī) does not depend on testing.

The shift to the name Allah apparently gives the rationale: faith, guidance, and reward all return to the One from whom things begin, by whom they subsist, and to whom they truly return. Therefore genuine faith cannot remain indistinguishable from an empty claim before Him.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan takes “those who commit misdeeds” in this context to mean the polytheists who persecuted believers and barred them from God’s way. Their supposed outmaneuvering of God is their attempt to thwart Him through this persecution and obstruction. “Evil is the judgement that they make” rejects their calculation: their scheme is itself a divine test that cuts them off from happiness, and an evil scheme harms its makers.

The commentary rejects the view that the verse specifically rebukes sinful believers for sins other than shirk, since it does not suit the tenor. Although “commit misdeeds,” considered in isolation, may be general enough to include polytheism and other sins, the verse’s contextual meaning is determined by the sūrah’s purpose and concerns the persecuting polytheists.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains (29:5-7) as returning to the person who claims faith after rebuking both those who abandon it under persecution and those who persecute believers. A genuine believer expects to return to and encounter God; without the Resurrection, religion would have no purpose. “Encountering God” (liqāʾ allāh) is the servant’s standing before his Lord without a veil on the Day of Resurrection, when realities become manifest. The reported explanations that make it arrival in the afterlife, meeting the Angel of Death, recompense, or divine judgement are figurative explanations of its implications rather than its original meaning; likewise, rajāʾ need not be made to mean fear.

“Allah’s time” is the appointed deadline for this encounter, not merely its duration, and it will certainly come. Since this foreordained Day cannot be disregarded, one who professes faith must speak sincerely, hold firmly to it, and be ready to endure trials. God’s being All-hearing and All-knowing means that He hears their profession and knows their states and deeds.

“To strive” (mujāhada and jihād) is to expend energy. Striving and steadfastness benefit the servant alone, for Allah has no need of any creature’s faith or action. The verse’s replacement of striving with faith and righteous deeds apparently shows that striving for God consists in these. Those who have faith and do righteous deeds will have their misdeeds forgiven—takfir al-sayyiʾāt means forgiveness, not the replacement of former disbelief with faith and disobedience with obedience—and will be rewarded according to their best deeds. This may mean elevation to the level merited by their finest acts, or that even deeds containing deficiencies will be treated as though performed in the best manner.

verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains tawṣiyya here as a divine command: human beings are commanded to treat their parents kindly. The use of ḥusnan, a verbal noun in the place of an adjective or as an intensification, emphasizes the goodness of this command.

The direct address—“if they urge you to ascribe to Me as partner”—makes unambiguous that parents must not be obeyed when they call one to associate partners with God. Such association follows what one has no knowledge of, is an embrace of ignorance (jahl), and invents a lie against God. The reminder that all return to God means that He will disclose the reality of their deeds, including idol worship and polytheism. The verse also subtly rebukes believers who abandoned their faith under parental pressure.
verses.9: Al-Mizan reads this as a reassuring promise to believers whose polytheist parents urge them toward association with God, but whom they disobey and, if necessary, separate from. Their loss of their parents entails no harm for them: through faith and righteous deeds, God will admit them among the righteous, the servants blessed with Paradise. The view that “the righteous” means a righteous society in this world does not fit the context.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan observes that God does not describe these people simply as possessing faith, but as saying, “We have faith in Allah,” because their supposed faith lasts only while they are safe and disappears under persecution. “Tormented in Allah” means tormented because of faith in God and the confession that one’s Lord is Allah. It should not be reduced to being tormented “in the way of God”: the latter concerns suffering because of one’s religious conduct, whereas the former concerns suffering on account of faith itself.

They evade human persecution as though it were God’s punishment, abandoning faith and returning to polytheism, even though human torment is fleeting and ends in escape or death, while God’s punishment brings everlasting ruin. Yet when relief or assistance comes to believers after hardship, they claim, “We were indeed with you,” seeking a share in it. The rhetorical question about what is in the breasts of the creatures rejects their claim, for Allah knows that their hearts contain no faith.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains that through trials God distinguishes believers from hypocrites. Those who profess faith as though it were unconditional but abandon it when persecuted are hypocrites, since testing believers is an unavoidable divine habit.

The commentary rejects the claim that the mention of hypocrisy, divine help, and jihād proves these verses or the sūrah Medinan. This is genuine hypocrisy: people claim faith and then renounce it under torment, something especially applicable to Mecca, where Muslims were persecuted, rather than Medina after the migration. Divine assistance (naṣr) is not restricted to conquest and spoils, and the verse does not state that such assistance has already occurred. The use of idha for persecution indicates its occurrence, while in for the coming of help indicates only its possibility. Moreover, “Whoever strives” refers to the struggle of the self (jihād al-nafs), not armed struggle against disbelievers. Thus nothing in these verses indicates a Medinan revelation.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan identifies the faithless as Meccan idolaters and the faithful as those who accepted the truth from the beginning. The idolaters’ invitation, “Follow our way and we will bear your iniquities,” seeks to bring believers back to polytheism by assuring them that it has no consequence—or, if it does, that the idolaters will bear every consequence on their behalf.

The verse categorically rejects this promise. If abandoning faith for the idolaters’ way is an iniquity, it belongs before God to the person who commits it, and its transfer to another would require God’s permission, since He alone punishes and requites it. Thus they will bear none of the believers’ iniquities. They are liars because their promise implicitly claims both that sins can be transferred merely by their agreement and that God will allow this.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains that the polytheists will not bear the believers’ actual sins, since each sin belongs to its doer. Rather, because they are themselves astray (ḍāll) and lead others astray (muḍill), they will bear burdens like those of the people whom they mislead, in addition to their own, without reducing those people’s burdens. On the Day of Resurrection they will be questioned about their fabrications: both their polytheism, which is a lie invented against God, and their false claim that they can relieve others of sin with God’s permission.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains ṭūfān as, most commonly, an immense overflowing mass of water, though it may denote anything that overwhelms through abundance and intensity, such as wind or darkness. “A thousand-less-fifty years” stresses the great number and plainly denotes Noah’s period of preaching, from the beginning of his mission until the Flood, rather than his lifespan as the present Torah states.
verses.15: Al-Mizan explains that Noah and the Ark’s occupants—his family and a small number of believing, non-wrongdoing people—were saved. It appears that the sign for later generations was the Flood or deliverance from it, rather than the Ark itself; “the worlds” means the many groups of people in subsequent generations.
verses.16: Al-Mizan takes the mention of Abraham as joined to Noah: God sent Abraham to his people. His command to worship Allah and be wary of Him is, in context, an invitation to Divine Unity and a warning of punishment. It therefore means worship and fear God alone, even without explicit particles of exclusivity, against idolaters who approached God through angels, jinn, and other supposed intermediaries.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan explains that awthān are idols and ifk is a distortion in word or deed. The indefiniteness of “idols” exposes their weakness and baseless supposed divinity: calling them gods and worshiping them is a lie, since worship belongs only to the One True God.

Idolaters sought benefit, especially provision, through representations of angels and jinn that they thought would bring them near to God. Yet these objects have no control (mulk) over provision, for God alone creates both people and their provision, and control follows creation and origination. They must therefore seek provision from God, worship Him rather than idols, and thank Him as their benefactor.

Their return to God supplies the ultimate reason for worship and gratitude: worldly provision has material causes and is not visibly increased or diminished by faith or unbelief, whereas happiness at the Resurrection depends on faith, worship, and thankfulness. Thus worship is not finally for worldly benefit but for the coming judgement.
verses.18: Al-Mizan holds that this is apparently still Abraham’s address to his people, not God’s address to the Quraysh. Their impugning of messengers is the recurrent habit of idolatrous nations, while a messenger’s duty is only clear communication. The verse may also mean that, like earlier deniers, they will gain nothing from denial when punishment comes: they cannot thwart God on earth or in heaven and have no guardian or helper. The final clause suits either reading.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan treats this as an aside answering deniers of the Resurrection. “Have they not regarded” calls all deniers to intellectual reflection on how God originates creation and then brings it back; the two verbs are jointly governed by “regarded,” not two separate rhetorical questions.

Origination and restoration are alike the bringing into existence of what was absent. Since God’s unrestricted power originated creation, restoring what He originated is easy; the return is the creature’s transfer from one abode to another and settlement in its final resting place before God. The interpretation that God merely creates another thing like the perished thing is rejected, because the Resurrection restores the very entity itself.
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is instructed to direct his opponents to travel and observe God’s originating of creation in its diverse temperaments, hues, appearances, numbers, and kinds, without a prior model or limiting constraint. This proves that nothing limits His power and that He can bring forth the creation of the Hereafter as readily as the first creation. The verse thus has the sense of: Certainly you have known the first genesis, then why do you not take admonition? (56:62)
verses.21:
Al-Mizan regards this as part of the Prophet’s instructed address and an exposition of the genesis of the Hereafter. The return to God is a return to life in a state of complete helplessness, where none controls benefit or harm and no judgement belongs to anyone but Him. Al-Mizan cites Majmaʿ al-Bayān’s interpretation of “turned” as “returned” in this sense.

The creation of the Hereafter is therefore the realm in which God punishes the wrongdoers and has mercy on the others, while all are returned to Him alone for judgement.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains that this remains part of the Prophet’s address and depicts people’s condition on the Day of Resurrection. They cannot evade God, escape His dominion, or hide anywhere in earth or heaven. The proposed reading that the heavenly clause concerns an omitted “whoever is in the sky” is unlikely, since the context does not indicate such an omission; even on that assumption, angels and jinn could have been included with humans by taghlīb.

They will have no guardian besides God to manage their affairs and make them independent of Him, nor any helper to reinforce them against Him. Thus neither they, nor another on their behalf, nor both together can escape or repel His punishment.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan holds that God now addresses the Prophet directly, rather than continuing the speech he was commanded to deliver. The repeated “those,” where direct address would say “you,” and the emphatic first-person phrase “My mercy” identify explicitly those destined for punishment, reassure the Prophet, and declare the deniers unworthy of hearing this news.

“Allah’s signs” comprehends all signs of monotheism, prophethood, and the Resurrection, including cosmic signs and prophetic miracles such as the Qur’an. The encounter with God is the Resurrection, singled out after the general category because denying it makes the question of true religion pointless. “Mercy” here means Paradise, the opposite of punishment. Their despair may describe their actual lack of hope in an afterlife, or God’s irrevocable decree that no faithless person enters Paradise. Thus those who deny the signs, especially the Resurrection, are deprived of divine mercy and face painful punishment.
verses.24: Al-Mizan explains that Abraham’s people discussed whether to kill him, apparently by the sword or the like, or burn him; groups may have proposed the alternatives, or they may initially have hesitated before agreeing on burning him. They ultimately built a bonfire, hurled him into it, and Allah saved him. The verse omits these details for brevity; the deliverance is a sign for believers.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan explains that Abraham addresses the masses, whose idolatry has no rational proof and rests on reverence for fathers, leaders, friends, and communal tradition. Their shared attachment both leads them to preserve idolatry and sustains their worldly cohesion. Some elites offer a purported rationalization—that God is too exalted to be directly worshiped and must be approached through angels or jinn as intermediaries—but it has no real basis.

The idols were taken as a means to achieve mutual worldly affection and communal life. Although “for the sake of affection” can grammatically express either the cause or the intended purpose of idolatry, the sequel favors the latter. On the Day when secrets are exposed, the companionship sought through this gravest wrongdoing becomes disavowal, mutual rebuke, and cursing. yakfur baʿḍukum bi baʿḍ means especially that the idols disown their worshippers; likewise, leaders disown followers, while all curse one another.

The Fire is their abode, without helpers to repel it. The affection through which they sought mutual support in this life thus becomes enmity and abandonment in the Hereafter.
verses.26: Al-Mizan explains that Lot believed in Abraham; the verb for belief may take either bi or li without a change of meaning. The speaker of “I am migrating toward my Lord” may be Lot or Abraham, though the latter is supported by He said: Indeed I am going toward my Lord, who will guide me (37:99). Migrating toward God means leaving one’s homeland and idolatrous people for a place where none prevents worship of the Lord. God’s being All-mighty and All-wise means that one He helps cannot be abased and one He protects cannot be lost.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that God gave Abraham Isaac and Jacob, established prophethood and the Book among his descendants, granted him his reward in this world, and will place him among the Righteous in the Hereafter.

Ajr is recompense for a deed, unlike ujra, which is confined to worldly wages; unlike jazāʾ, ajr is used only for what is good and beneficial. It usually denotes the believers’ otherworldly recompense for worship, including nearness to God, degrees of wilāya, and Paradise, but it can also denote a good worldly reward, as in the account of Joseph. Here the most suitable reading is that Abraham was actually granted a good worldly life, not merely that it was prepared or decreed for him. It is also possible that he received in this world spiritual stations otherwise reserved for the faithful in the Hereafter.
verses.28: Al-Mizan reads the verse as either “We sent Lot” or “mention Lot,” when he rebuked his people for an unprecedented indecency: seeking gratification with men. “None in the world has ever committed before you” may be an independent clarification emphasizing that this practice had never spread among a people in this way, or an adverbial qualifier of those committing it.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan takes Lot’s question as an emphatic expression of astonishment: they come to men for gratification, thereby neglecting women and marriage, the way of producing offspring; and they commit indecency, or its preliminaries, openly in their gatherings. The reported interpretations that “cut off the way” means attacking travellers, robbing and violating them, or brigandage generally, and that their gatherings contained every variety of sin, are not favored, since the context indicates the first meaning.

Their demand that Lot bring God’s punishment was mockery, but it also shows that he had warned them of punishment.
verses.30: Al-Mizan explains that Lot asks God for victory against a corruptive people. He calls them mufsidīn because their deeds corrupt the land by cutting off progeny and threatening humanity’s destruction.
verses.31: Al-Mizan summarizes that angels came first to Abraham, gave his wife the good news of Isaac and Jacob, and then announced their mission to destroy Lot’s town. “This town” suggests that it was near Abraham’s land, the Holy Land. The explicit repetition, “Its people are indeed wrongdoers,” explains both their destruction and the fact that wrongdoing had become a settled characteristic specific to them, warranting divine punishment.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan explains that Abraham’s words, “Lot is indeed in it,” sought to avert punishment from Lot’s people on account of Lot’s presence, not to secure Lot’s own rescue. Abraham knew that God would not destroy His appointed prophet, and he was not simply alarmed at the punishment. The angels replied to the apparent sense of his wording: they knew who was in the town and would save Lot and his family, except his wife, who was to remain behind.

Abraham was in fact pleading for the town’s people, as shown by: “So when the awe had left Abraham and the good news had reached him, he pleaded with Us concerning the people of Lot. Abraham was indeed most forbearing, plaintive, [and] penitent. O Abraham, let this matter alone! Your Lord’s edict has certainly come, and an irrevocable punishment shall overtake them (11:74–76).” The decree against them was irrevocable.
verses.33: Al-Mizan explains that the messengers caused Lot distress and difficulty because they appeared as two handsome young men. He feared that his people would harm them and, when they sought to do so, could not protect guests under his care. Their assurance means that he faced no danger: fear concerns anticipated harm, while grief concerns harm already suffered. They would save him and his family, except his wife, who would remain behind in the punishment.
verses.34: Al-Mizan explains that rijz is the punishment from the sky which the messengers had implied when promising to deliver Lot and his family. It would descend on the town’s people because of their persistent transgressions.
verses.35: Al-Mizan explains that “We have left of it” means that God kept the village’s ruins as a manifest sign, so that rational people might take warning and fear God. Although its precise site is now unknown and no trace remains—some suggest it was submerged to form the Dead Sea—the verse emphatically indicates that it was known and visible when the Qur’an was revealed, as do Indeed it is on a standing road (15:76) and And indeed you pass by them at dawn and at night. So do you not apply reason? (37:137–138).
verses.36: Al-Mizan explains that Shuʿayb called Midian to worship Allah—that is, to Divine Unity (tawḥīd)—to believe in the Resurrection by expecting the Last Day, and to cease corrupting the land. According to Qur’anic accounts mentioned elsewhere, their principal corruption was tampering with marketplace weights and scales.
verses.37: Al-Mizan explains that rajfa is a violent shaking, while jathm and juthūm, literally sitting or kneeling in place, euphemistically denote death. Shuʿayb’s people denied him, so an earthquake left them dead and motionless in their homes. The account elsewhere that the Cry seized them suggests that both a cry and a quaking destroyed them.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan takes the accusative mention of ʿAd and Thamud as implying, “Remember ʿAd and Thamud.” Satan’s making their deeds seem decorous is a metaphor for making them love evil and become attached to it; by this he turned them from God’s way, the way of fiṭra.

Although some take their former perceptiveness to mean adherence to simple human nature, that state belonged before Noah, whereas ʿAd and Thamud came after him. Their former perceptiveness therefore means that, before Satan led them astray, they lived in God’s worship and the faith of Divine Unity, the religion of fiṭra.
verses.39: Al-Mizan explains that Korah, Pharaoh, and Haman acted arrogantly despite Moses’ manifest proofs. Their inability to “outmaneuver” means that they could not defeat God.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains that each of the preceding nations was seized for its own sin: a ḥāṣib, meaning stones—though it is also said to be a wind carrying pebbles—struck Lot’s people and, in the latter sense, ʿAd; the Cry seized Thamud and Shuʿayb’s people; the earth swallowed Korah; and drowning overtook Noah’s people and Pharaoh, Haman, and their people.

These punishments were not divine injustice but the recompense of their own wrongdoing. This world is an abode of trial and tribulation, an inescapable divine habit: whoever is guided is guided for his own sake, and whoever strays does so only against himself.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that the idolaters’ taking guardians besides God resembles a spider’s taking a home: a spider’s web is called a house only in name, for it gives neither shelter nor protection. Likewise, their supposed guardians possess guardianship only in name: they cannot benefit or harm, nor control life, death, or resurrection.

They are called awliyāʾ rather than gods because the idolaters rely on them for the management of their affairs, hoping for benefit, protection from evil, and intercession. In its unrestricted sense, the parable applies to anyone who entrusts an affair to a guardian besides God and expects an independent effect from it, even if it is not regarded as an idol. It does not apply where such wilāya is understood to fall under God’s guardianship, as with the wilāya of God’s Messenger, the Imams, and the faithful. “Had they known” means that, had they recognized this likeness, they would not have taken guardians besides God.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan holds that mā in mā yadʿūna min dunihi min shayʾin may be read in several ways, though the relative-pronoun sense, “what they invoke besides Him,” is strongest. On this reading, God’s knowledge of their objects of invocation confirms the aptness of the preceding parable: their guardianship is merely nominal. On the possible negative reading, God knows that they invoke nothing real besides Him, so their gods are wholly unreal; as the author of al-Kashshāf says, this reinforces the spider parable.

God’s names All-mighty and All-wise establish that no one shares His dominion, creation, or origination, and that His perfect governance is not delegated to another. This prepares for the explanation that creation of the heavens and earth is with reason.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan says that the verse concerns all Qur’anic parables: they reach everyone, but only people of knowledge grasp their realities and highest lessons rather than remaining caught by appearances. The wording says that only such people “grasp” them, not merely that they believe them; people thus receive parables according to their levels, from hearing only their sound and surface meaning to probing their deepest purposes.

The spider image is consequently not a poetic comparison or an empty assertion. The likeness between idolaters’ guardians and the spider’s frail home rests on a verified reality and a logical argument, indicated by the following verse.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah’s creation of the heavens and earth “with reason” (bi al-ḥaqq) excludes play or triviality. Creation follows a fixed, unchanging divine order; creation and governance are inseparable, since governing phenomena through an ordered system is itself the bringing of one thing after another into being.

Everything besides God is created by Him, subsists through Him, and belongs to Him; it has no independent power over benefit or harm, either for itself or for another. Thus no creature can exercise independent guardianship or possess a share in dominion (mulk). To delegate governance to a creature would be play (laʿb), a false supposition incompatible with creation’s reality and earnestness. The guardianship invoked by idolaters is therefore no more truly guardianship than a spider’s web is truly a house. Though this sign applies universally, only the faithful benefit from it.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains that reciting the revealed Book deters idolatry, indecency, and evil through its proofs, stories, lessons, admonitions, promises, and warnings. The command to maintain prayer follows because prayer is the best of deeds and, by its very nature, restrains its performer from indecencies and wrongs. This restraint does not mean an absolute prevention of every sin; sustained, sincere prayer develops a fixed habit (malaka) of aversion to wrongdoing in both thought and action.

Prayer repeatedly recalls God’s oneness, prophethood, and the Hereafter; it places the servant before his Lord in worship, seeking guidance and refuge from misguidance and wrath. It directs body and soul toward God’s praise and glory, and requires purification and avoidance of usurped clothing or place before facing the House of God. Repeated reverent concentration (tawajjuh ʿibādī), especially within a righteous society, thus trains the soul away from major sins and from what sound conscience and upright human nature reject.

The commentary considers the objection that many frequent prayers do not visibly prevent grave sins. It rejects interpreting ṣalāt as supplication or calling people to God because that abandons the verse’s apparent meaning. It also finds inadequate the explanations that only some prayers have this effect, that restraint lasts only during the prayer, that prayer merely issues a prohibition like a person saying “do not do it,” or that even a sinful worshipper would have been worse without prayer. The verse instead identifies the soul’s formation of a restraining habit as prayer’s essential natural effect.

This effect is consequential (iqtiḍāʾī), not inevitable like the effect of a sufficient cause. Impediments may weaken remembrance and distract the worshipper; the more complete one’s presence of mind, fear, and pure devotion, the stronger prayer’s restraint, and the weaker these are, the weaker it becomes. This is reflected in the contrast between those who abandon prayer and consequently neglect other obligations and distinctions of purity, lawfulness, and unlawfulness, those who perform its minimum obligation and have greater self-control, and those who take prayer more seriously and are still more averse to sin.

Al-Mizan distinguishes dhikr as recalling and making present in heart or speech what is known: ḥifẓ concerns retaining knowledge, while dhikr concerns recalling it. Spoken remembrance is called dhikr because it brings the meaning into the heart; remembrance of the heart is its effect and goal. Prayer is dhikr through its verbal glorification, praise, and exaltation of God, and because it produces the heart’s remembrance that is its intended outcome.

The phrase “and the remembrance of Allah is surely greater” therefore adds an effect of prayer greater than its deterrence from sin: the heart’s awareness of God, the greatest human good, the key to every good, and the felicity prepared for humanity. It is also possible that “remembrance” means the verbal remembrance within prayer, or prayer itself; even then it is greater than the single beneficial effect of preventing indecency and wrongdoing. In either case, “greater” is understood as greater than that prevention.

The commentary reports and largely dismisses as arbitrary competing readings: that God’s remembrance of His servant is greater than the servant’s remembrance, prayer, or everything else; that a servant’s dhikr is greater than other elements of prayer, his dhikr at other times, or his other deeds; that prayer surpasses all obedience; that remembrance at the point of sin is a greater deterrent; or that akbar has no comparative force. Finally, Allah’s knowledge of every good and evil deed commands vigilance (murāqaba), particularly in connection with the reading concerning God’s remembrance of His servant.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains that, in teaching how the Qur’an is to be preached, the verse commands disputation with the People of the Book—including Jews, Christians, Zoroastrians, and Sabeans—only in the best manner. Such disputation excludes coarse speech, insult, and ridicule; it uses courtesy and kindness without provoking the other side, and proceeds through shared cooperation to discover the truth without prejudice or obstinacy.

The exception for wrongdoers concerns those for whom friendliness and cooperation bring no benefit: they take good manners as lowliness or as a scheme to strip them of their beliefs. With those open to discussion, the Qur’an directs the speakers to begin from their common ground: belief in what was sent down to both communities, in one God, and in submission to Him.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan takes “Thus have We sent down the Book to you” primarily to mean that the Qur’an was sent down with the description of submission (islām) to God and belief in His scriptures and messengers. A proposed alternative—that it simply compares the Qur’an’s descent to the earlier scriptures sent to Moses and Jesus—is reported.

Those previously given the Book believe in the Qur’an because it calls to the God, scriptures, and messengers in whom they already believe. “Of these” refers independently to idol-worshipping polytheists, some of whom also believe in it. None of either group contests the signs except the faithless, who cover truth with falsehood. The alternative identification of those given the Book as Muslims and “these” as the People of the Book, as well as the view that “it” refers to the Prophet, is considered unlikely.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan explains that recitation (tilāwah) here apparently means reading from a written book, and that mubṭilūn most suitably means those who call truth false, though it can also mean those who introduce falsehood in speech. The verse more appropriately denies the Prophet’s prior habit of reading and writing than his capacity to do so: before the Qur’an, he did not customarily read other scriptures or write them.

The reference to the right hand intensifies the statement. Because the Prophet was unschooled (ummī), and his contemporaries had known throughout his life that he neither read nor wrote, the impugners have no basis for alleging that the Qur’an was assembled from previous scriptures and their stories. Had he had such a habit, their skepticism would have had an apparent justification; his condition instead supports the Qur’an’s truthfulness and divine descent.
verses.49: Al-Mizan says that the verse prevents the inference from the Prophet’s not reading or writing that the Qur’an is merely a written, bound book. Rather, the Qur’an consists of manifest signs in the breasts of those given knowledge. Those who contest these signs are wrongdoers in the sense that they wrong the signs by obstinately and arrogantly denying them.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains that the demand for signs other than the Qur’an shows the opponents’ disregard for the Qur’an as the sign of prophethood. Their wording, asking why signs have not been “sent down” to him rather than asking him to bring them, is mocking; it also assumes that a messenger must possess powers by which he can produce whatever he wishes.

The commanded reply rejects this assumption. Signs belong exclusively to Allah, who sends them down when and as He wills, and the Prophet has no share in that power. His role is only that of a manifest warner.
verses.51: Al-Mizan explains that the rhetorical question answers the claim that the Qur’an is not itself a sign. The Book sent down to the Prophet should suffice them as a sign: when it is recited to them, its miraculous character is evident, and it contains mercy and admonition for those who have faith.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah is the sufficient witness in the dispute over prophethood because He testifies to Muḥammad’s prophethood through the word He has sent down, while His knowledge encompasses everything in the heavens and earth. This is not an empty rhetorical claim: the opponents cannot maintain that the Qur’an is not God’s word when they have repeatedly been challenged to produce its like.

Those who deny the Qur’an thereby deny God, who is the Truth, and necessarily place faith in falsehood. Their loss follows from this faith in falsehood and defiance of Allah.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan explains that the demand to hasten punishment repeats the insolence of earlier peoples who challenged their messengers to bring it. The specified time (ajal musammā) is the term decreed for Adam’s earthly abode and for every nation, a term that cannot be advanced or delayed.

The withheld punishment is what they deserve for all their evil deeds; God does not immediately take them to task because they have an appointed tryst and no refuge from Him. This does not contradict His sending the signs demanded from a messenger and thereby removing grounds for reprieve or delay. When the appointed punishment comes, it will overtake them suddenly while they are unaware.
verses.54: Al-Mizan explains that the repeated demand to hasten punishment exposes the faithless’ ignorance: they seek to accelerate what has been decreed and cannot be rushed, and they seek a punishment that cannot be averted because it follows inseparably from their own deeds. Hell will besiege them, and the punishment will envelop them from every side, above and beneath their feet. The phrase concerning the day of this enveloping specifies the time when hell surrounds them.
verses.55: Al-Mizan explains that the repeated demand to hasten punishment exposes the faithless’ ignorance: they seek to accelerate what has been decreed and cannot be rushed, and they seek a punishment that cannot be averted because it follows inseparably from their own deeds. Hell will besiege them, and the punishment will envelop them from every side, above and beneath their feet. The phrase concerning the day of this enveloping specifies the time when hell surrounds them.
verses.56:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse addresses believers living in a land of disbelief where they cannot openly practise the true religion. God’s earth, arḍ, is the dwelling-place of humankind and belongs wholly and equally to Him, so He may be worshipped anywhere upon it. Its vastness means that being prevented from practising the religion in one region does not make worship impossible, since another region remains available.

The first fāʾ in fa iyāya fa ʿbudūn draws the conclusion from the earth’s vastness, while the second introduces the result of an implied condition: if this is so, worship Me. The advance placement of iyāya apparently signifies exclusivity. Thus believers must worship God alone, not anyone besides Him; if they cannot do so in one place, they must migrate elsewhere and worship Him there.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan states that this verse reinforces the command to worship God alone and prepares for the description of those who are patient and trust their Lord (29:59). “Every soul shall taste death” metaphorically declares that every soul will die, while the shift to directly addressing the listener in “Then you shall be brought back to Us” inspires awe.

Worldly life is only a few days before death and return to God for reckoning. Its fleeting trinkets must not distract people from preparing through faith and righteous deeds, which bring everlasting happiness; neglecting them brings never-ending ruin.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan explains that, after death and return to God, those with faith and righteous deeds will be settled permanently in lofty abodes, ghurafa, in paradise, with streams flowing beneath them. To settle is to establish someone as a resident, and ghurafa is the plural of ghurfa, an upper-floor room. The verse thereby encourages believers to bear hardship for God and rely upon Him.

Having first named faith and righteous deeds, the verse calls their possessors “workers” (ʿāmilīn); the following description, “Those who are patient and who put their trust in their Lord…” (29:59), identifies patience (ṣabr) and reliance on God (tawakkul) as special qualities of the faithful. Faith is accepted only when the believer endures hardship for God’s sake and trusts Him. He must therefore bear every worldly difficulty and pain in God’s way; if practising the religion becomes impossible in his land, he must depart for another land, accepting suffering and deprivation for God’s sake.
verses.59: Al-Mizan explains that this describes the workers: patience (ṣabr) includes enduring hardship, fulfilling obligations, and avoiding sins. In this context, however, it particularly concerns enduring hardship, as suits the believers in Mecca who are commanded to emigrate.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains that “How many” (ka ayyin) denotes abundance, and that carrying provision means storing it, as humans and certain creatures do. The verse reassures believers who emigrate for God’s sake that He will provide for them wherever they go: they need not fear hunger, because their provider is their Lord, not their homeland. Many animals do not carry stored provision, yet God sustains them, and He likewise sustains humans who do store food.

The closing names, the All-hearing and the All-knowing, provide the proof. Humans and every other creature are existentially needy of God and entreat Him for provision; He hears their prayers and knows their needs. It therefore follows from these names that He will provide for them.
verses.61: Al-Mizan explains that the creation of the heavens and earth and the origination and disposal of the sun and moon—including their rising, setting, and changing distance from the earth—underlie the sustenance of humans and animals. Creation and governance (al-khalq wa al-tadbīr) are inseparable: whoever acknowledges one must acknowledge the other. Since God alone creates and governs the cosmos and the provision of its creatures, He alone should be asked for provision and every other form of disposal. The question, “Then where do they stray?” therefore exposes the absurdity of invoking and worshipping powerless idols besides Him.
verses.62: Al-Mizan explains that God expands provision for some servants and measures it, that is, restricts it, for others. He wills this only according to His creatures’ best interests (maṣlaḥa), which He knows through His knowledge of all things. The verse’s use of Allah rather than a pronoun indicates that His all-encompassing knowledge belongs to Him because He is God, absolutely perfect in every respect.
verses.63: Al-Mizan explains that reviving the earth after its death is the flourishing of vegetation in spring. The idolaters themselves admit that Allah sends down the rain and thereby governs His creation; “All praise belongs to Allah” praises God for completing the proof against them through this admission, which requires them to worship Him alone rather than idols or the deities they claim the idols represent. Most nevertheless do not apply reason, since they neither reflect on the signs nor properly use their intellects to know God and distinguish truth from falsehood.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan explains diversion (lahw) as what distracts from something important, and play (laʿb) as a purposeless organized activity. Worldly life is diversion because its fleeting vanities distract from the eternal Hereafter, and play because it soon vanishes like a children’s game. The objects for which people compete—such as wealth, spouses, children, rank, leadership, and power—are often illusory, existing only in their imaginations.

The Hereafter, by contrast, is the life in which a person dwells in the real perfection acquired through faith and righteous deeds. It contains no diversion, play, futility, or blame: it is endless life, pleasure without pain, and happiness without grief. Thus it alone is life in the fullest sense. The verse’s demonstrative “this” lowers worldly life, while its emphatic wording identifies the Hereafter with life itself. “Had they known” means that, if they possessed knowledge, they would recognize this reality.
verses.65: Al-Mizan presents this as a further proof of the idolaters’ straying and failure to apply reason: in danger at sea they invoke Allah with exclusive faith, yet once He brings them safely to land they ascribe partners to Him. They acknowledge a truth but deny its necessary consequence, thereby contradicting themselves and showing ingratitude for God’s blessings. The wording for boarding the ship conveys remaining aboard it or continuing to ride upon it, emphasizing their condition at sea.
verses.66: Al-Mizan holds that the lām in li yakfurū and li yatamattaʿū is best read as the imperative lām. When God commands what displeases Him, the command is a threat and warning, like: Act as you wish; indeed He sees best what you do (41:40). It is possible instead to take it as purposive, meaning that they act in order to be ungrateful for God’s blessings and to enjoy themselves. But the imperative reading accords better with “Soon they will know!” and is supported by: Let them be ungrateful toward what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves! Soon you will know! (30:34). Some accordingly recite the lām vowelless, as only the imperative lām may be vowelless.
verses.67: Al-Mizan identifies the safe sanctuary as Mecca and its environs, made a sanctuary in answer to Abraham’s prayer. While the Arabs lived amid continual fighting, looting, and enslavement, they respected the sanctuary and did not attack those dwelling there. Thus God asks whether they do not consider that He made them secure from killing, looting, and enslavement while people around them suffered such depredations. They are rebuked for answering this great blessing with ingratitude and belief in idols, which are only mere names.
verses.68: Al-Mizan explains that the verse threatens the Meccan idolaters with hell for the gravest wrongdoing: fabricating a lie against God by alleging that He has partners, and denying the truth when it came to them. Since they worshipped idols and denied the Qur’an, both descriptions apply to them; they are truly disbelievers, whose abode in the Hereafter is hell.
verses.69:
Al-Mizan explains that mujāhada means expending one’s full effort in repelling an enemy. Al-Rāghib reports three varieties of striving: against a manifest foe, Satan, and one’s own self. To “strive in Us” figuratively means that one’s efforts in belief and action are connected with God, so that nothing turns one away from faith, obedience to His commands, or observance of His prohibitions; it need not be interpreted as an implicit expression meaning “for Our sake.”

God’s ways (subul) all lead to Him, since a way is a means of reaching its destination; they are therefore the paths that bring people near to God and guide them toward Him. Since striving itself is guidance, being guided to these ways is guidance upon guidance, as indicated by: As for those who are guided, He enhances their guidance (47:17).

Some interpret God’s being with the virtuous as His assistance and support, an interpretation plausibly suggested by the mention of striving. Al-Mizan prefers to understand it as symbolic of His mercy and concern, which includes assistance and support as well as other forms of care shown to His virtuous servants. This is more particular than His general being with all things by virtue of their existence, expressed in: …and He is with you wherever you may be… (57:4). The verse also fittingly concludes the sūrah in relation to its opening.
